subject: arts-music
unit_title: Advanced Studio Practice and Personal Direction
lesson_title: Concept model A: advanced composition and visual hierarchy
task_label: Visual art concept — Build intentional hierarchy
standards: Michigan Arts Education Standards: Visual Arts — Creating
essential_question: How can an artist direct attention without telling the viewer where to look?
learning_objectives: Build a clear mental model of advanced composition and visual hierarchy from an explicit worked example, demonstration, or source.
Communicate understanding of advanced composition and visual hierarchy using subject-appropriate evidence or representation.
Check, revise, or improve the work on advanced composition and visual hierarchy against the stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task on advanced composition and visual hierarchy.
The learner supplies evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.
The learner checks or revises the work and can name a next step.
materials: Required: one sheet of plain or scrap paper and a pencil, pen, or accessible digital mark-making tool.
Household-accessible route: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough.
Approved alternatives: a reusable drawing surface, three moveable paper shapes, raised-line shapes, or a tactile board.
Optional enhancements: markers, coloured pencils, collage paper, or a preferred drawing application; polish and colour never affect credit.
Supplied reference: the Academy-original annotated model and its full text description are included with this lesson.
task_brief: Today you will investigate visual hierarchy: the order in which a composition asks the eye to notice its parts. You will see one composition develop from a flat arrangement into an intentional route, test one variable in a small guided study, and then build a fresh composition with your own focal point and visual path. Your subject, style, mood, and final revision remain your choices.
primary_task: Study the supplied visual model for advanced composition and visual hierarchy. First, notice how placement, value contrast, scale, repetition, and a directional line change the order of attention. Next, complete two quick guided thumbnails while changing only placement; compare which shape you notice first and cite the visual evidence. Then create an independent composition from three or more forms. Choose your own focal point, use at least two hierarchy variables, record one intermediate state, ask a viewer to trace the visual path or run the private blur-and-glance check yourself, and make one learner-chosen revision. Finish with a criteria-based reflection and self-critique. You are not expected to copy the model's shapes, arrangement, colours, or mood.
requirements: Complete the placement-only guided study before the independent composition.
In the independent work, choose one focal point and use at least two of these variables: value contrast, scale, placement, isolation, repetition, edge, or directional line.
Preserve one intermediate state with a thumbnail, tracing-paper overlay, duplicate digital layer, or brief written map of what changed.
Use the stated intent and observable evidence—not similarity to the model or anyone's personal taste—to choose one revision.
Complete the reflection and critique blocks; a private self-critique receives full credit.
deliverable: Two guided thumbnails, one original composition study, one preserved intermediate state, a visual-path check, one learner-chosen revision, and a short reflection and critique.

ATTACHED MANUEL ACADEMY LEARNER RESOURCE

Resource ID: ma-resource:ma-g9-arts-and-music-u01-l02
Lesson focus: advanced composition and visual hierarchy

Title: Three Stops — an annotated visual-hierarchy model
Creator: Manuel Academy curriculum team
Role: technique model, worked artistic example, partial exemplar, and one possible finished exemplar

The delivered SVG shows three stages on warm white panels. Stage 1 is a flat start: a small circle, medium striped rectangle, and large pale triangle have similar visual weight, so no first stop is clear. Stage 2 changes placement, scale, and value: a small nearly black circle sits high left with open space around it; a striped rectangle sits near the centre; a large pale triangle touches the lower right edge. Stage 3 adds a thin curved line from circle to rectangle to triangle. Numbered annotations mark an intended eye path of 1 circle, 2 rectangle, 3 triangle. A second mini-composition reverses the priority with a large dark triangle at upper right, proving that the model's exact arrangement is not the answer.

Technique sequence: begin with a stated focal point; arrange large masses; create the strongest useful difference at the focal point; repeat or direct a feature to build a path; step back or blur-and-glance; revise one variable at a time. Common trouble spot: increasing every contrast equally can make all parts compete. Recovery: return most areas to quieter values or edges, then retest the intended first stop.

Access parallel: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough. For a tactile route, use three raised or cut-paper shapes. Make one shape noticeably rougher, taller, or more isolated than the others, then connect the shapes with string. Trace the route by touch and name the order. The tactile and described routes teach the same relationship without making colour discrimination carry the criterion.

critique_criteria: The submission includes two placement studies, an original composition, one intermediate state, and one documented revision.
The learner names the intended focal point and uses at least two visual-hierarchy variables in ways that can be located in the work.
The learner cites observable evidence for the visual path and explains how the evidence relates to the stated intent.
The revision responds to a check or critique while remaining the learner's choice; difference from the model is never penalized.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. You may keep the work private, show it to one trusted adult, or submit the artwork alone with no person in view. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or recording is required, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available for every spoken note and scores the same. You may describe the visual path, label a diagram, or ask a trusted adult to verify the physical work. Because the target is visual hierarchy, the artwork, tactile arrangement, or accessible digital composition must still show the spatial relationship being studied; prose alone does not claim visual-making evidence.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. The composition and revision must be your own. An adult, tutor, or AI tool may explain visual hierarchy, demonstrate on a separate example, restate a criterion, or ask a noticing question, but must not draw, arrange, revise, or finish the work being scored. Use original, public-domain, or openly licensed material and cite any source you choose to add. The supplied model is Academy-original and may be studied or adapted, but your result is not expected to match it.
accessibility_options: Use enlarged, high-contrast, raised-line, cut-paper, tactile, or accessible digital forms while keeping the hierarchy target unchanged.
Work in short intervals, hide the suggested time, reduce copying, or use a low-distraction setting without a scoring penalty.
Record reflection by typing, handwriting, dictation to a trusted adult, or labelled marks; no voice or camera capture is required.
Use the full text description and tactile route alongside the visual model; colour is always paired with value, texture, scale, or position.
task_accessibility_provisions: The required SVG includes high-contrast forms, pattern as well as value differences, descriptive title and alternative text, and a complete adjacent verbal description.
A tactile route uses three raised or cut-paper forms plus string; relative size, texture, spacing, and touch order preserve the visual-hierarchy relationship.
Breaks, extended time, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Use only safe, familiar mark-making tools; place scissors or cutting tools aside unless an adult has approved and supervised their use.
Stop or change tools if a grip, posture, light, or material causes discomfort.
Keep the work private if you prefer; no image of you, your room, or your identifying information is required.
Critique the evidence and choices in the work, never talent, character, effort, or personal taste.

media.fallback: Use the supplied full verbal description and the tactile three-shape-and-string route. The reference is a committed Academy asset, not a teacher-supplied or outside-search requirement.

remediation: If the intended focal point does not become the first clear stop, use the supplied value-map route: label each major area 1 (light), 2 (middle), or 3 (dark), circle the largest jump, then make a fresh three-form thumbnail with one strong jump at the intended focal point and quieter differences elsewhere. If every part competes, cover all but two areas and restore them one at a time, keeping only the differences that serve the intended route. If the route is clear but differs from the model, no correction is needed. After either repair, run a fresh three-second glance check and record what arrived first; do not erase the earlier attempt.
extension: Optional depth: create a second composition with the same forms but a different intended focal point. Change only two hierarchy variables, compare the two visual paths, and explain the tradeoff. The second composition is never required for full credit.

concept_registry.meaning: The arrangement and relationship of parts within the edges of a work.
The order in which a composition invites attention.
The area an artist intends as the strongest or first stop.
The open area around and between forms, used here to create isolation.
A bounded visual or tactile area used as a compositional element.
Relative spatial priority among nearer and farther areas of a composition.

Create emphasis by controlling relative size without assuming largest must lead.
Create emphasis through location, spacing, clustering, and isolation.

age_policy.language: Direct, discipline-specific Grade 9 language with new terms defined at first use.
age_policy.safety: Familiar household mark-making tools, no pain-based coaching, and no unsupervised cutting requirement.
age_policy.privacy: Private work and self-critique carry full credit; no public display or identifiable media is required.

vocabulary.definition: the arrangement and relationship of parts within the edges of a work
the order in which a composition invites attention
the area an artist intends as the strongest or first stop
a difference between light and dark
open space that separates one element from a group

concept_instruction.title: Hierarchy is an order, not an object
concept_instruction.body: A focal point is not automatically the largest thing or the thing in the centre. It becomes important because it differs from its surroundings. The largest jump in value, scale, detail, edge, direction, or spacing often creates the first stop. Repetition and directional lines can then carry attention to later stops.

concept_instruction.title: Variables work in relation
concept_instruction.body: A small dark form can outweigh a large pale form when its value jump and isolation are stronger. Increasing every contrast at once usually flattens the hierarchy because every area competes. Quiet areas are active choices: they give stronger areas room to lead.

concept_instruction.title: Clarity has a tradeoff
concept_instruction.body: A very steep hierarchy can make the first stop immediate but later areas easy to ignore. A shallow hierarchy can feel open or calm but may not support a precise route. Neither is automatically better; the evidence must be compared with the artist's stated intent.

reference_registry.title: Three Stops — verbal and tactile description
reference_registry.creator: Manuel Academy curriculum team

model_registry.notice: Similar visual weight leaves the first stop unsettled.
model_registry.creator_choice: Use similar mid-values and even spacing as a deliberate non-example.

model_registry.notice: Isolation and the largest value jump make the small circle arrive first.
model_registry.creator_choice: Keep the large triangle pale so size does not automatically win.

model_registry.notice: A curved directional line and repeated stripe angle carry attention through three stops.
model_registry.creator_choice: The circle-first route is one solution; the alternate panel makes a triangle-first route with different choices.

technique_sequence.action: State the intended first, second, and third stops before making.
technique_sequence.notice: The order gives you something testable instead of a vague goal.
technique_sequence.why: Hierarchy is judged in relation to intent.

technique_sequence.action: Place the largest masses and leave some areas quiet.
technique_sequence.notice: Check negative space—the open area around forms—not only the forms.
technique_sequence.why: Placement and isolation establish structure before detail distracts you.

technique_sequence.action: Make one useful difference strongest at the intended focal point.
technique_sequence.notice: Look for the largest jump in value, scale, edge, texture, or direction.
technique_sequence.why: Difference creates emphasis only in relation to nearby areas.

technique_sequence.action: Build a route using repetition, alignment, overlap, or a directional line.
technique_sequence.notice: Trace where your eye or hand moves after the first stop.
technique_sequence.why: A composition can organize later attention as well as the focal point.

technique_sequence.action: Step back or blur-and-glance for three seconds, then revise one variable.
technique_sequence.notice: Record what arrived first before explaining or judging it.
technique_sequence.why: Changing one variable makes the effect of the revision easier to read.

work_blocks.title: Guided study — move the first stop
work_blocks.prompt: Make two 8–10 cm thumbnails with the same three simple forms. In A, cluster the forms evenly. In B, move one form away from the others. Keep size and value as similar as you can.
work_blocks.bounded_choice: Choose which form to isolate and where to place it.
work_blocks.observable_criterion: Your notes identify which form arrives first in each thumbnail and cite spacing or placement as evidence.
work_blocks.attempt_before_support: Complete both thumbnails and record a first impression before opening the placement cue.
work_blocks.optional_cue: If the isolated form still does not lead, enlarge the open space around it without darkening or enlarging the form.
work_blocks.support_fade: Close the model and cue before beginning the independent composition.

work_blocks.title: Independent studio — design a visual path
work_blocks.prompt: Choose a subject or use abstract forms. Plan three possible thumbnails, select one, and develop a composition with an intended first, second, and third stop.
objective_constraints: Use three or more forms or areas.
Name one intended focal point before developing the study.
Use at least two hierarchy variables.
Run one visual-path check and make or deliberately decline one revision with a reason.
learner_owned_choices: whether critique evidence calls for revision
work_blocks.permitted_support: Definitions, the technique sequence, a parallel example, material alternatives, and criterion restatement remain available. No one else may choose the focal point or alter the scored composition.

work_blocks.title: Reflection — trace your decisions
prompts: Name your intended first, second, and third stops. Cite one visible feature at each location.
Compare your preserved intermediate state with the later state. What variable changed, and what did that change do?
Which tradeoff did you accept: a steeper route with quieter later areas, or a subtler route with more openness? Explain from the work.

work_blocks.title: Private critique — evidence before advice
protocol: Describe the first area noticed without judging it.
Point to the contrast, spacing, scale, edge, repetition, or direction that produced that stop.
Compare the observed path with the artist's stated intent.
Ask one genuine question about the route.
Offer two revision possibilities; the artist may choose either, invent another, or keep the work with evidence.
work_blocks.private_route: Use the protocol on your own work after turning it away for one minute. No peer, audience, or public post is required.

work_blocks.title: Knowledge check — explain the mechanism
prompts: A large pale form and a small dark isolated form share a page. Give two reasons the small form might arrive first.
Why can increasing contrast everywhere weaken an intended hierarchy?
Name one situation in which a subtle hierarchy could serve an artist's intent better than a steep one.
work_blocks.note: This check supports concept understanding but does not replace the independent visual work.

common_technique_errors.observable_mismatch: Several major areas use similarly strong value jumps, hard edges, or detail, so the intended focal point is not a reliably distinct first stop.
common_technique_errors.not_an_error_when: The learner states and supports an intent for distributed, ambiguous, or nonhierarchical attention.

common_technique_errors.observable_mismatch: The learner names a focal point, but two separate three-second checks identify another area first and the learner cannot cite a hierarchy variable supporting the intended area.
common_technique_errors.not_an_error_when: The learner revises the stated intent to match a defensible observed route.

remediation_paths.different_instruction: Reduce the work to a three-value map. Label each major area light, middle, or dark; circle every large jump. Keep one large jump and lower the others in a fresh thumbnail.
remediation_paths.supported_attempt: Use three forms and only pencil pressure. Create one dark-light jump at the intended first stop; keep the other forms middle or pale.
remediation_paths.self_noticing_cue: Squint or use the tactile value labels: can you locate one strongest difference?
remediation_paths.fresh_retry: Make a new thumbnail with different placements and run a new three-second check.

remediation_paths.different_instruction: Cover the work except for the intended focal point and one competing area. Compare only those two; choose whether value, scale, isolation, edge, or direction should separate them.
remediation_paths.supported_attempt: On scrap paper, redraw the two areas and change exactly one chosen variable.
remediation_paths.self_noticing_cue: Name the changed variable before deciding which area arrives first.
remediation_paths.fresh_retry: Return all areas in a fresh thumbnail and test the intended path without the model in view.
